title: Nahum 3:12–19
context: The prophet tells Nineveh that her fortresses will be like first-ripe figs, falling into the eater’s mouth when shaken, and that the gates of the land stand open to the enemy, the bars already burned. She is told to draw water for the siege and strengthen the brickwork, yet fire and sword will devour her, as the grasshopper is devoured. Her merchants are more than the stars, but the grasshopper strips and flees; guards and officials are like locusts that settle on a cold day and flee when the sun appears. The king of Assyria is addressed: the shepherds slumber, the nobles lie down, the people are scattered on the mountains with no one to gather them. The wound has no healing and is fatal, and all who hear the report clap their hands, for they have felt her endless cruelty.

verses.text: All your fortresses will be like fig trees with the first-ripe figs. If they are shaken, they fall into the mouth of the eater.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All your fortresses will be like fig trees with the first-ripe figs. If they are shaken, they fall into the mouth of the eater.” The fortresses are first-ripe figs: a shake, and they fall into the eater’s mouth. The image is of something ready and easy to take, a defense that will not hold. The falling is told in that comparison, and it is not enlarged.

Arminian readers hear a warning about trust in fortresses, a ripeness for taking that the city may still recognize, a word that treats the walls as already ready to fall.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the fig-tree fortresses, the shaking, and the fall into the eater’s mouth as the LORD’s appointed ease of the city’s fall.

Shared ground: the fortresses will fall like first-ripe figs. The image is the verse’s own, and it is enough.

verses.text: Behold, your troops among you are women. The gates of your land are set wide open to your enemies. The fire has devoured your bars.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Behold, your troops among you are women. The gates of your land are set wide open to your enemies. The fire has devoured your bars.” The verse pictures the troops as unable to hold the gates, which stand open to the enemy, and the bars already burned. The comparison is the oracle’s own, a line about failed defense, and it is told in that one sentence.

Arminian readers hear open gates and burned bars, a defense that has already failed, a word that still names the failure as the city’s own condition before the enemy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the open gates, the burned bars, and the failure of the troops as the LORD’s appointed opening of the land to the enemy.

Shared ground: the gates are set wide open, and the fire has devoured the bars. The line is about a defense that does not hold.

verses.text: Draw water for the siege. Strengthen your fortresses. Go into the clay, and tread the mortar. Make the brick kiln strong.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Draw water for the siege. Strengthen your fortresses. Go into the clay, and tread the mortar. Make the brick kiln strong.” The city is told to prepare: draw water, strengthen fortresses, tread mortar, make the kiln strong. The commands sound like a last effort at brick and cistern. They sit beside the open gates of the verse before, and they will sit beside the fire of the verse after.

Arminian readers hear a call to work that cannot, in this oracle, outrun the sentence, a siege preparation that still treats the city as one who will try to hold on, and will not succeed by brick.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the drawing of water, the strengthening of fortresses, and the work in clay and kiln as ironic commands, the last labors of a city whose end is already spoken.

Shared ground: she is told to prepare for siege. The next verse will say what the fire and the sword will do.

verses.text: There the fire will devour you. The sword will cut you off. It will devour you like the grasshopper. Multiply like grasshoppers. Multiply like the locust.
verses.arminianNotes:
“There the fire will devour you. The sword will cut you off. It will devour you like the grasshopper. Multiply like grasshoppers. Multiply like the locust.” Fire and sword devour, like the grasshopper is devoured, even as she is told to multiply like grasshopper and locust. The locust image begins here and runs on through the next verses: great numbers that can still be swept away.

Arminian readers hear a devouring that numbers cannot prevent, a call to multiply that is already under the fire and the sword, a word that still uses the city’s own size against a false hope in plenty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the fire, the sword, the devouring like the grasshopper, and the command to multiply like locusts as the LORD’s appointed end of her numbers.

Shared ground: fire and sword will devour her, even if she multiplies like the locust. The insect figure continues in the lines that follow.

verses.text: You have increased your merchants more than the stars of the skies. The grasshopper strips and flees away.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You have increased your merchants more than the stars of the skies. The grasshopper strips and flees away.” Merchants are more than the stars, and the grasshopper strips and flees. The trading plenty is set beside an insect that eats and is gone. The wealth of the markets will not stay.

Arminian readers hear a commerce as countless as the stars, stripped in a moment, a fleeing that leaves the increase behind, a word against trust in merchants and in scale.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the merchants more than the stars, and the grasshopper that strips and flees, as the LORD’s appointed emptying of the city’s trade.

Shared ground: the merchants were increased, and the grasshopper strips and flees. Plenty is no protection.

verses.text: Your guards are like the locusts, and your officials like the swarms of locusts, which settle on the walls on a cold day, but when the sun appears, they flee away, and their place is not known where they are.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Your guards are like the locusts, and your officials like the swarms of locusts, which settle on the walls on a cold day, but when the sun appears, they flee away, and their place is not known where they are.” Guards and officials are locusts on a cold wall, gone when the sun appears, their place unknown. The people whose task was to keep the city vanish with the warmth of the day.

Arminian readers hear a leadership that settles only while it is convenient, a flight when the day turns, a word that still names guards and officials as responsible, and as gone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the locust-guards, the swarms of officials, the settling on the cold wall, and the flight when the sun appears as the LORD’s appointed failure of the city’s keepers.

Shared ground: when the sun appears, they flee, and their place is not known. The locust figure now fits the officials themselves.

verses.text: Your shepherds slumber, king of Assyria. Your nobles lie down. Your people are scattered on the mountains, and there is no one to gather them.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Your shepherds slumber, king of Assyria. Your nobles lie down. Your people are scattered on the mountains, and there is no one to gather them.” The king of Assyria is addressed at last. Shepherds slumber, nobles lie down, and the people are scattered on the mountains with no one to gather them. The flock is without a gatherer, and the titles of rule are names of sleep.

Arminian readers hear a king spoken to in the second person, a charge that the shepherds have slept and the people are scattered, a word that still treats the king as accountable for an ungathered people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the address to the king of Assyria, the slumbering shepherds, the nobles who lie down, and the ungathered people on the mountains as the LORD’s appointed end of that rule.

Shared ground: the king of Assyria is named, and the people are scattered with no one to gather them. The book’s last human addressee is this king.

verses.text: There is no healing your wound, for your injury is fatal. All who hear the report of you clap their hands over you, for who hasn’t felt your endless cruelty?
verses.arminianNotes:
“There is no healing your wound, for your injury is fatal. All who hear the report of you clap their hands over you, for who hasn’t felt your endless cruelty?” The wound cannot be healed; the injury is fatal. Those who hear the report clap their hands, because they have felt her endless cruelty. The close is the oracle’s own verdict on unhealed cruelty, and the clapping is explained by that cruelty, not left as empty joy.

Arminian readers hear a fatal wound and a world that has felt the cruelty, a last “who hasn’t felt” that still treats the nations as witnesses with a real grievance, and the book as a moral close, not a song of mere revenge.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the unhealable wound, the fatal injury, the clapping of those who hear the report, and the endless cruelty as the LORD’s own last word over Assyria.

Shared ground: the injury is fatal, and the cruelty has been felt. The book ends on that verdict.
